An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01Sk1nEx4urQGX5Rac4RG9U8","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\nis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n\n## 5. Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. If any is wrong, the phase order changes, so please confirm:**\n1. **The 50 services already exist and ship through older pipelines.** If they don't, there are no migration waves, Phase 4 becomes onboarding, and V5/V6 go away.\n2. **Every service deploys to Kubernetes.** If some don't, the deploy-model row in §3 changes for them.\n3. **The code lives on GitHub.**\n4. **No audit regime (SOX/SOC 2/PCI) is confirmed yet.** If one applies, approval separation and change-record evidence move into Phase 2.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A shared build, test, sign and deploy path (golden path) that 50 existing services move onto in waves. It replaces their separate pipelines.\n- **Type:** Infrastructure plus some software (pipeline templates and policy code). Brownfield. Not small: many teams, an R3 trust-boundary decision, and it deploys to production for real users.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness and security of what reaches production. Production availability comes second, because one shared deployer can hit all 50 services at once.\n- **Worst failure:** The platform becomes the way an unreviewed or malicious artifact reaches production across many services, either through a compromised CI job, credential or pipeline definition, or through a template bug pushed to the whole fleet. Guarded by V1, plus release rings for template changes (Phase 2).\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Commit-to-prod lead time; change failure rate; time to restore | No worse than today's numbers for the same services | BASELINE (measured in Phase 0 from 90 days of CI/VCS history). An improvement target is UNKNOWN: engineering leadership sets it, needed by Phase 4 | V5 |\n| PR check feedback time | p90 < 15 min | ASSUMPTION (how long developers will usually wait; confirm with engineering leadership) | V2, V5 |\n| Runner queue time | p95 < 2 min at 2× measured peak load | ASSUMPTION (same basis) | V3 |\n| Throughput (peak concurrent jobs, merges per day) | — | UNKNOWN: the platform team pulls it from 90 days of CI history in Phase 0; V3 needs it | V3 |\n| Platform availability | CI: 99.5% in business hours. Rollback must still work when CI or Git is down | ASSUMPTION (a CI outage delays work but doesn't break prod; confirm with engineering leadership) | Phase 3 game day |\n| Detect and roll back a bad deploy | p95 < 10 min | ASSUMPTION (compare with BASELINE time to restore; confirm with SRE) | V4 |\n| RPO / RTO | Registry RPO 0 for any image digest that has run in prod. Platform rebuilt from code in < 4 h | ASSUMPTION (rollback needs the prior image; the 4 h is a starting value) | Phase 3 DR test |\n| CI compute + storage cost | — | UNKNOWN: monthly CI budget from engineering finance. Requested in Phase 0, needed by V3 | V3 |\n| Operational complexity | Self-run components ≤ 3 (Argo CD, policy controller, External Secrets); everything else managed | ASSUMPTION (a platform team of about 4; the real size is a missing input) | Phase 3 exit |\n\n**Missing inputs:** the four assumptions above; platform team size; the number of clusters, regions and environments; the improvement target; the CI budget; how long build and audit records must be kept (needed by V6).\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Skeleton prod deploy (Phase 0) | Cluster and cloud access for the platform team; change approval for a new deploy path. ASSUMED needed | Organizational | Deployed |\n| Pull-based deploy default (§3) | Phase 0 inventory confirms all deploy targets are Kubernetes. ASSUMED | Decision | Specified |\n| V3 pass | CI budget figure from engineering finance | Organizational / economic | Passing (UNKNOWN threshold) |\n| Larger runner fleet; wave 2 onward | V3 | Economic / validation | Committed |\n| Any service beyond the skeleton and the 3 pilots | V1 sign-off by the security lead (book the review in Phase 0; it takes time to schedule) | Risk-security / organizational | Exposed |\n| Template 1.0 freeze; all waves | V2 | Validation | Specified / hardened |\n| Tier-1 services (wave 3); fleet-wide auto-rollback | V4 | Validation | Exposed |\n| Each service's cutover | A slot from its team and that service's secrets inventory | Organizational | Deployed (its wave) |\n| Next wave | V5 for the previous wave | Validation | Exposed |\n| Shutting down the old CI | V6. Old-CI dependents (cron jobs, release scripts, compliance exports, chatops) are ASSUMED to exist until the Phase 0 inventory confirms them | Risk / organizational | Committed (irreversible) |\n| Compliance evidence in templates | Confirmation of the audit regime | Organizational | Specified |\n| V2 pilots | 3 service teams agree to take part | Organizational | Built (Phase 2) |\n\nThe phase order already shows the structural and runtime dependencies (registry and Argo CD before deploys; the trust model before templates).\n\n**Inherited constraints (not changing; cost to change):**\n- GitHub as code host: months, every repo and integration.\n- Existing clusters and cloud account: months.\n- One repo per service: months, every team.\n- Service languages and architecture: out of scope; no re-architecting during the move.\n- The existing metrics and alerting stack: reused; switching would take weeks.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Deploy trust boundary: push (CI holds prod credentials) vs pull | R3: once exposed, a compromise can't be undone | Pull: Argo CD in each cluster syncs from an environment repo. CI only pushes signed images and opens PRs. No prod credentials in CI. One Argo CD project per team, CODEOWNERS on each team's environment-repo paths | Targets are Kubernetes | V1 | V1 fails, or the inventory shows non-Kubernetes targets. Then push for those targets, with short-lived per-environment OIDC roles |\n| Secrets and data-privacy boundary | R3: a leaked secret or personal record can't be un-leaked | Secrets live in the cloud secret manager and reach pods at runtime through External Secrets. CI gets short-lived OIDC credentials. Log masking. Push protection for secrets. No prod data in CI; tests use synthetic data | Services can read secrets at runtime | V1 | V1 finds a way to read prod secrets from a branch workflow |\n| Consistency vs availability of desired state | R2: changes the deploy process for every team | Git is the only deploy path. A logged, time-boxed emergency path (break-glass) can roll back to an image already in the registry | Git or CI outages are rare and short | Phase 3 game day: with CI down, rollback finishes in < 15 min and the drift is written back to Git | Game day fails, or break-glass is used more than twice a quarter. Then add an Argo history-based rollback that doesn't need Git |\n| Platform shape (monolith vs services) | R2: 50 repos follow its interface | One shared golden path (versioned reusable workflows plus Argo CD), with a documented escape hatch. No custom platform API | 80% or more of services fit a few language profiles | V2 | V2 fails on coverage. Then per-stack template families |\n| Sync vs async checks; how services are tested together | R2: changes how teams work together | PR checks run synchronously (≤ 15 min). Long suites run after merge, before prod. Compatibility between services is checked with consumer-driven contract tests (Pact), not lockstep releases in a shared environment | Most bugs between services show up at the API contract | V2 measures PR duration | V5 shows integration bugs raising change failure rate above BASELINE. Then pull in per-PR ephemeral environments |\n| Build vs buy (CI engine and runners) | R2: moving CI systems takes weeks | GitHub Actions on GitHub-hosted runners, managed registry, Argo CD. Build only the templates and policy | Hosted runners meet queue time and budget | V3 | V3 fails. Then self-hosted runners managed by Actions Runner Controller (ARC) on a dedicated CI cluster |\n| Deploy strategy | R2: needs per-service metrics | Rolling deploy with automatic health checks for all. Argo Rollouts canary with automated analysis for tier-1 | Tier-1 services have usable error-rate and latency signals | V4 | V4 fails. Then manual promotion for tier-1 |\n| Migration, coexistence, rollback, system of record | R2 per service; shutdown is irreversible | Move each service's pipeline onto the templates; the services themselves don't change. Exactly one pipeline is active per service. The old pipeline is frozen, not deleted. The system of record for \"what's deployed\" is the old pipeline until cutover, then the environment repo | Services can switch one at a time | V5 per wave; V6 for shutdown | A wave fails V5. Then pause and re-plan that wave |\n\n**R1 defaults:** container build with BuildKit and registry cache; Terraform for the platform's own code; Renovate for template version bumps; distroless base images; Slack for alerts; third-party actions pinned to commit SHAs.\n\n**N/A:** AI rows (no AI component).\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request and response:** A real commit merged to one low-criticality, stateless service with a willing owner. It is built, signed (audit mode only), pushed to the registry by digest, synced to staging and smoke-tested. Then the same digest is promoted by an environment-repo PR and synced to prod. A real user request to that service returns the new version in a response header.\n- **Tiers:** GitHub → Actions workflow v0 → OIDC → managed registry → environment repo → Argo CD (staging, then prod) → service → existing metrics stack.\n- **How it runs on day zero:**\n  - Platform built with Terraform through its own pipeline.\n  - Pipeline and Argo events go to metrics, with deploy markers on the service's dashboard.\n  - Alerts fire on failed sync, degraded health or a failed pipeline, and page the platform on-call.\n  - Rollback: `git revert` in the environment repo. Full fallback: detach the Argo app without deleting anything and re-enable the frozen old pipeline.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only this one service is allow-listed. Argo is scoped to that service's namespace. The service's users are the same users as before. No other team can use the templates yet. Branch protection and review rules are kept as strict as the old path.\n- **Also in Phase 0 (read-only or organizational):**\n  - Inventory all 50 services: stack, deploy target, secrets, tier, owner.\n  - List everything that depends on the old CI, each marked CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n  - Measure the baselines in §1.\n  - Request the CI budget, the security review date and the audit-regime answer.\n\n**V0** = the standard exit check: a real deploy and a rollback through the pipeline, one trace across every tier, an injected failure (a bad image tag in staging) fires an alert, and first values are recorded as low-load baselines.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 1 — Trust boundary and supply chain** (most rework if wrong: all 50 services inherit it)\n- **Unlocks:** exposing the platform beyond the skeleton (via V1).\n- **Depends on:** V0.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. OIDC from CI to the cloud; remove every long-lived credential.\n  2. CODEOWNERS and required reviews on workflow files, templates and environment-repo paths. Fork PRs get no secrets.\n  3. One Argo CD project per team.\n  4. Keyless cosign signing plus SLSA provenance. Admission policy enforced in prod for migrated namespaces, audit-only elsewhere (so services not yet migrated aren't blocked).\n  5. Secret manager plus External Secrets, push protection, log masking.\n  6. Write and rehearse the break-glass procedure.\n  7. Secret scan of the history of all 50 repos; rotate whatever it finds.\n- **Rollback:** put admission back in audit mode; re-enable old credentials (kept sealed until V6).\n- **Exit check:** V1.\n\n**Phase 2 — Template contract and capacity**\n- **Unlocks:** template 1.0 and committing to runners (via V2, V3).\n- **Depends on:** Phase 1, the budget input.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Define the template interface (`service.yaml`: owner, tier, profile, test commands) and language profiles that cover ≥ 80% of the inventory.\n  2. Version templates with semver, keep N-1 working, roll out bumps through Renovate.\n  3. Release rings for template changes: pilot repos → 10% → all.\n  4. Run V2 with 3 mixed pilots: the most common stack, an unusual one, and one with DB migrations.\n  5. Run V3.\n- **Rollback:** pilot repos pin the previous template version or go back to their old pipeline.\n- **Exit check:** V2, V3.\n\n**Phase 3 — Deploy safety and platform resilience**\n- **Unlocks:** tier-1 migration (via V4).\n- **Depends on:** V2.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Automatic health checks and rollback.\n  2. Argo Rollouts canary for tier-1 profiles.\n  3. Per-service lead time, deploy frequency, failure rate and restore-time dashboards.\n  4. Argo CD and policy controller in HA, registry replication, a retention rule that never deletes a digest that has run in prod.\n  5. Game days for CI, Git and registry outages.\n  6. DR test: rebuild the platform from Terraform within the RTO.\n  7. Run V4.\n- **Rollback:** turn off auto-rollback or canary per profile.\n- **Exit check:** V4, game day and DR targets met, operational-complexity cap held.\n\n**Phase 4 — Migration waves** (smallest exposure first)\n- **Unlocks:** the whole fleet on the platform.\n- **Depends on:** V1, V2; V3 before wave 2; V4 before wave 3.\n- **Waves:** wave 1 = 5 low-criticality services; wave 2 = about 20; wave 3 = the rest, tier-1 last.\n- **Before each service cuts over:** secrets moved and scan clean; new pipeline run in shadow next to the old one for 1 week with matching test results; team briefed.\n- **At each cutover:** freeze the old pipeline, Argo takes ownership, enforce admission in that namespace, revoke the old pipeline's prod credentials only after the V5 window.\n- **Rollback:** per service, re-enable the old pipeline (the system of record goes back to it).\n- **Exit check:** V5 per wave.\n\n**Phase 5 — Shut down the old CI**\n- **Depends on:** V5 for all waves.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Move or retire every old-CI dependent from the inventory.\n  2. Export build and audit records to the archive.\n  3. Power off the old CI for 2 weeks (still reversible).\n  4. Run V6, then delete.\n- **Point of no return:** deleting the old CI and its credentials, guarded by V6.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in prod | §4 run on the skeleton service | The V0 exit check in §4 | Trace ID, deploy and rollback run links, alert record, baseline sheet in the platform repo | Phase 1 | 0 |\n| V1 | A compromised CI job or pipeline change can't put an unreviewed artifact into prod or read prod secrets | Red-team test of 5 attacks: fork PR deploy; CI token writing to the prod cluster or prod environment paths; unsigned or outside image applied to a prod namespace; branch workflow reading prod secrets; cross-team environment-repo write. If it fails: ARC self-hosted runners | 2; required before wave 2 |\n| V4 | A bad deploy is caught and rolled back automatically without false alarms | 10 injected bad builds (failed readiness, error spike at 5% canary) on the skeleton and pilot services; 2 weeks of normal deploys | 10/10 rolled back, p95 < 10 min (ASSUMPTION); 0 false rollbacks in 2 weeks | Rollout analysis logs and game-day report | Tier-1 wave and fleet-wide auto-rollback. If it fails: manual promotion for tier-1 | 3 |\n| V5 | Each wave is no worse on the new path | Compare each wave's services for 2 weeks after cutover | Change failure rate and lead time p50 ≤ the same services' BASELINE; 0 sev-1 incidents caused by the platform | Wave scorecard (dashboard export) | Next wave. If it fails: pause, roll back the worst services, fix | 4, per wave |\n| V6 | The old CI can be deleted safely | Power-off rehearsal plus inventory check | All 50 on the new path for ≥ 30 days; 0 old-pipeline runs in 30 days; 100% of dependents moved or retired; records archived for the retention period (UNKNOWN: compliance/legal supplies it before Phase 5); approved by the platform lead, security lead and engineering director | Signed go/no-go record, archive manifest | Deletion. CI only pushes signed images and opens PRs. No prod credentials in CI. One Argo CD project per team, CODEOWNERS on each team's environment-repo paths | Targets are Kubernetes | V1 | V1 fails, or the inventory shows non-Kubernetes targets. Then push for those targets, with short-lived per-environment OIDC roles |\n| Secrets and data-privacy boundary | R3: a leaked secret or personal record can't be un-leaked | Secrets live in the cloud secret manager and reach pods at runtime through External Secrets. CI gets short-lived OIDC credentials. Log masking. Push protection for secrets. No prod data in CI; tests use synthetic data | Services can read secrets at runtime | V1 | V1 finds a way to read prod secrets from a branch workflow |\n| Consistency vs availability of desired state | R2: changes the deploy process for every team | Git is the only deploy path. A logged, time-boxed emergency path (break-glass) can roll back to an image already in the registry | Git or CI outages are rare and short | Phase 3 game day: with CI down, rollback finishes in < 15 min and the drift is written back to Git | Game day fails, or break-glass is used more than twice a quarter. Then add an Argo history-based rollback that doesn't need Git |\n| Platform shape (monolith vs services) | R2: 50 repos follow its interface | One shared golden path (versioned reusable workflows plus Argo CD), with a documented escape hatch. No custom platform API | 80% or more of services fit a few language profiles | V2 | V2 fails on coverage. Then per-stack template families |\n| Sync vs async checks; how services are tested together | R2: changes how teams work together | PR checks run synchronously (≤ 15 min). Long suites run after merge, before prod. Compatibility between services is checked with consumer-driven contract tests (Pact), not lockstep releases in a shared environment | Most bugs between services show up at the API contract | V2 measures PR duration | V5 shows integration bugs raising change failure rate above BASELINE. Then pull in per-PR ephemeral environments |\n| Build vs buy (CI engine and runners) | R2: moving CI systems takes weeks | GitHub Actions on GitHub-hosted runners, managed registry, Argo CD. Build only the templates and policy | Hosted runners meet queue time and budget | V3 | V3 fails. Then self-hosted runners managed by Actions Runner Controller (ARC) on a dedicated CI cluster |\n| Deploy strategy | R2: needs per-service metrics | Rolling deploy with automatic health checks for all. Argo Rollouts canary with automated analysis for tier-1 | Tier-1 services have usable error-rate and latency signals | V4 | V4 fails. Then manual promotion for tier-1 |\n| Migration, coexistence, rollback, system of record | R2 per service; shutdown is irreversible | Move each service's pipeline onto the templates; the services themselves don't change. Exactly one pipeline is active per service. The old pipeline is frozen, not deleted. The system of record for \"what's deployed\" is the old pipeline until cutover, then the environment repo | Services can switch one at a time | V5 per wave; V6 for shutdown | A wave fails V5. Then pause and re-plan that wave |\n\n**R1 defaults:** container build with BuildKit and registry cache; Terraform for the platform's own code; Renovate for template version bumps; distroless base images; Slack for alerts; third-party actions pinned to commit SHAs.\n\n**N/A:** AI rows (no AI component).\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **Request and response:** A real commit merged to one low-criticality, stateless service with a willing owner. It is built, signed (audit mode only), pushed to the registry by digest, synced to staging and smoke-tested. Then the same digest is promoted by an environment-repo PR and synced to prod. A real user request to that service returns the new version in a response header.\n- **Tiers:** GitHub → Actions workflow v0 → OIDC → managed registry → environment repo → Argo CD (staging, then prod) → service → existing metrics stack.\n- **How it runs on day zero:**\n  - Platform built with Terraform through its own pipeline.\n  - Pipeline and Argo events go to metrics, with deploy markers on the service's dashboard.\n  - Alerts fire on failed sync, degraded health or a failed pipeline, and page the platform on-call.\n  - Rollback: `git revert` in the environment repo. Full fallback: detach the Argo app without deleting anything and re-enable the frozen old pipeline.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only this one service is allow-listed. Argo is scoped to that service's namespace. The service's users are the same users as before. No other team can use the templates yet. Branch protection and review rules are kept as strict as the old path.\n- **Also in Phase 0 (read-only or organizational):**\n  - Inventory all 50 services: stack, deploy target, secrets, tier, owner.\n  - List everything that depends on the old CI, each marked CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n  - Measure the baselines in §1.\n  - Request the CI budget, the security review date and the audit-regime answer.\n\n**V0** = the standard exit check: a real deploy and a rollback through the pipeline, one trace across every tier, an injected failure (a bad image tag in staging) fires an alert, and first values are recorded as low-load baselines.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n**Phase 1 — Trust boundary and supply chain** (most rework if wrong: all 50 services inherit it)\n- **Unlocks:** exposing the platform beyond the skeleton (via V1).\n- **Depends on:** V0.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. OIDC from CI to the cloud; remove every long-lived credential.\n  2. CODEOWNERS and required reviews on workflow files, templates and environment-repo paths. Fork PRs get no secrets.\n  3. One Argo CD project per team.\n  4. Keyless cosign signing plus SLSA provenance. Admission policy enforced in prod for migrated namespaces, audit-only elsewhere (so services not yet migrated aren't blocked).\n  5. Secret manager plus External Secrets, push protection, log masking.\n  6. Write and rehearse the break-glass procedure.\n  7. Secret scan of the history of all 50 repos; rotate whatever it finds.\n- **Rollback:** put admission back in audit mode; re-enable old credentials (kept sealed until V6).\n- **Exit check:** V1.\n\n**Phase 2 — Template contract and capacity**\n- **Unlocks:** template 1.0 and committing to runners (via V2, V3).\n- **Depends on:** Phase 1, the budget input.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Define the template interface (`service.yaml`: owner, tier, profile, test commands) and language profiles that cover ≥ 80% of the inventory.\n  2. Version templates with semver, keep N-1 working, roll out bumps through Renovate.\n  3. Release rings for template changes: pilot repos → 10% → all.\n  4. Run V2 with 3 mixed pilots: the most common stack, an unusual one, and one with DB migrations.\n  5. Run V3.\n- **Rollback:** pilot repos pin the previous template version or go back to their old pipeline.\n- **Exit check:** V2, V3.\n\n**Phase 3 — Deploy safety and platform resilience**\n- **Unlocks:** tier-1 migration (via V4).\n- **Depends on:** V2.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Automatic health checks and rollback.\n  2. Argo Rollouts canary for tier-1 profiles.\n  3. Per-service lead time, deploy frequency, failure rate and restore-time dashboards.\n  4. Argo CD and policy controller in HA, registry replication, a retention rule that never deletes a digest that has run in prod.\n  5. Game days for CI, Git and registry outages.\n  6. DR test: rebuild the platform from Terraform within the RTO.\n  7. Run V4.\n- **Rollback:** turn off auto-rollback or canary per profile.\n- **Exit check:** V4, game day and DR targets met, operational-complexity cap held.\n\n**Phase 4 — Migration waves** (smallest exposure first)\n- **Unlocks:** the whole fleet on the platform.\n- **Depends on:** V1, V2; V3 before wave 2; V4 before wave 3.\n- **Waves:** wave 1 = 5 low-criticality services; wave 2 = about 20; wave 3 = the rest, tier-1 last.\n- **Before each service cuts over:** secrets moved and scan clean; new pipeline run in shadow next to the old one for 1 week with matching test results; team briefed.\n- **At each cutover:** freeze the old pipeline, Argo takes ownership, enforce admission in that namespace, revoke the old pipeline's prod credentials only after the V5 window.\n- **Rollback:** per service, re-enable the old pipeline (the system of record goes back to it).\n- **Exit check:** V5 per wave.\n\n**Phase 5 — Shut down the old CI**\n- **Depends on:** V5 for all waves.\n- **Tasks:**\n  1. Move or retire every old-CI dependent from the inventory.\n  2. Export build and audit records to the archive.\n  3. Power off the old CI for 2 weeks (still reversible).\n  4. Run V6, then delete.\n- **Point of no return:** deleting the old CI and its credentials, guarded by V6.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in prod | §4 run on the skeleton service | The V0 exit check in §4 | Trace ID, deploy and rollback run links, alert record, baseline sheet in the platform repo | Phase 1 | 0 |\n| V1 | A compromised CI job or pipeline change can't put an unreviewed artifact into prod or read prod secrets | Red-team test of 5 attacks: fork PR deploy; CI token writing to the prod cluster or prod environment paths; unsigned or outside image applied to a prod namespace; branch workflow reading prod secrets; cross-team environment-repo write. Plus a credential inventory | Sign-off by the security lead: all 5 denied and logged; 0 long-lived cloud credentials in CI; every secret-scan finding rotated | Red-team report, admission-denial logs, credential inventory (kept in the security repo, not CI) | Wave 1. If it fails: flip the §3 trust rows, fix and re-test | Review booked in 0; run in 1; required before 4 |\n| V2 | One versioned template fits the fleet | 3 mixed pilots build and deploy through template 1.0-rc; a major version bump goes out through Renovate | 0 template forks; ≤ 50 lines of pipeline config per repo (ASSUMPTION: more means the template isn't absorbing variation); PR p90 < 15 min (ASSUMPTION) and ≤ each pilot's BASELINE; profiles cover ≥ 80% of inventory (ASSUMPTION) | Pilot report and per-repo config diff in the platform repo | Freezing template 1.0 and the waves. If it fails: per-stack template families | 2 |\n| V3 | Hosted runners meet queue time within budget | Replay 2× the measured peak concurrency as synthetic jobs for 2 h; project monthly cost from the bills | Queue p95 < 2 min (ASSUMPTION); projected cost ≤ budget (UNKNOWN until finance supplies it; requested in Phase 0) | Load-test report and cost projection | Wave 2 and fleet scale-up. If it fails: ARC self-hosted runners | 2; required before wave 2 |\n| V4 | A bad deploy is caught and rolled back automatically without false alarms | 10 injected bad builds (failed readiness, error spike at 5% canary) on the skeleton and pilot services; 2 weeks of normal deploys | 10/10 rolled back, p95 < 10 min (ASSUMPTION); 0 false rollbacks in 2 weeks | Rollout analysis logs and game-day report | Tier-1 wave and fleet-wide auto-rollback. If it fails: manual promotion for tier-1 | 3 |\n| V5 | Each wave is no worse on the new path | Compare each wave's services for 2 weeks after cutover | Change failure rate and lead time p50 ≤ the same services' BASELINE; 0 sev-1 incidents caused by the platform | Wave scorecard (dashboard export) | Next wave. If it fails: pause, roll back the worst services, fix | 4, per wave |\n| V6 | The old CI can be deleted safely | Power-off rehearsal plus inventory check | All 50 on the new path for ≥ 30 days; 0 old-pipeline runs in 30 days; 100% of dependents moved or retired; records archived for the retention period (UNKNOWN: compliance/legal supplies it before Phase 5); approved by the platform lead, security lead and engineering director | Signed go/no-go record, archive manifest | Deletion. If it fails: keep it powered off and fix the gaps | 5 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | OIDC to the registry; Argo limited to one namespace; branch protection; signing in audit mode | Pipeline and deploy metrics, deploy markers, alerts, baselines | Platform in Terraform; pinned action SHAs; build once, promote the same digest | Old pipeline as fallback; revert-based rollback tested |\n| 1 | V1 controls | Code-host audit log, Argo, admission denials and break-glass events go to the SIEM, masked like the data they record | Signed provenance per image | Break-glass rehearsed; admission controller HA so rollback still works |\n| 2 | Template repo owned by platform and security; signed template releases; SBOMs | Pipeline duration and failure metrics per template version; queue dashboard | Semver templates, lockfile-keyed caches | Template release rings; N-1 support |\n| 3 | Tier policy (tier-1 must canary) | Canary SLI analysis; per-service delivery-metrics dashboards | DR rebuild from code | HA, registry replication, game days |\n| 4 | Secrets moved and rotated per service; old prod credentials revoked after V5 | Wave scorecards against baseline | Each service pins a template version | One wave at a time; per-service rollback to the old pipeline |\n| 5 | Revoke every old-CI credential and account | Watch for calls to old-CI endpoints for 2 weeks | Archive export of build records | Power off before deleting; snapshot restore tested |\n\n## 8. AI layer\nN/A: no AI component.\n\n## 9. Methodology exceptions\nNone.\n\n## 10. Deliberately deferred\n- **Developer portal (Backstage):** pull forward when the fleet passes about 100 services or teams struggle to find services.\n- **Per-PR ephemeral environments:** pull forward when V5 shows integration bugs driving change failures (§3 flip).\n- **ARC self-hosted runners:** pull forward when V3 fails or tests need private network access.\n- **Blocking builds on critical CVEs from SBOMs:** pull forward once the scanner's false-positive rate has been measured on 2 waves.\n- **Merge queues:** pull forward when main-branch breakage on any service goes above about 1 in 20 merges.\n- **Per-team cost showback:** pull forward when runner spend passes 80% of budget.\n- **Multi-region active-active platform:** pull forward when a region outage blocking deploys breaks a stated RTO.","ttft_ms":3332,"type":"result","duration_ms":291032,"uuid":"0c7ada1a-e40d-4fd7-899e-4707dc2dcf7b","ttft_stream_ms":2329,"time_to_request_ms":195,"first_content_frame_ms":2335,"queued_turn_count":0,"result_index":0}
